heading: CHAPTER XVIII.
title: CONCERNING THE WAY IN WHICH PRINCES SHOULD KEEP FAITH
exclusions: front matter and dedication before THE PRINCE
notes: Chapter 18 argues that praiseworthy fidelity is not sufficient for rule because princes contend by both law and force, and successful rulers often know how to use craft when good faith would be turned against them.

The chapter's core distinction is between possessing virtues and appearing to possess them. Machiavelli makes appearance politically decisive because people judge more by sight and result than by direct knowledge.
The limit is not casual lying. The prince should not depart from the good if he can avoid it, but should know how to turn when necessity and the maintenance of the state compel it.
